7.model: A firewall alone is a single barrier: if it is breached, nothing else stands between the attacker and everything inside the network. Defense in depth layers several measures, each at a different point: a firewall at the network entry, a VPN on the communication path, a DMZ for server placement, and antivirus and updates on the endpoints. If one measure is breached, the next can still protect the system — for example, an attacker who gets into a public web server in the DMZ still cannot reach the internal database. So a single failure is far less likely to expose the whole network.
points: A firewall alone is one barrier (1)
If that one barrier is breached, everything inside is exposed (1)
Defense in depth layers several measures (1)
Names at least two layers or measures, e.g. VPN, DMZ, endpoints (1)
If one is breached, the next still protects the system (1)
Conclusion: one breach is much less likely to expose the whole network (1)

8: 1. A VPN creates an encrypted virtual private line (a tunnel) over the Internet for safe connection from a remote location. Uses: remote work (connecting from home or while away) and connecting branches (offices in different places).

2. In a DMZ, the public server is separated from the internal network, so if it is attacked the attacker cannot go on to the internal network and its confidential data. Inside the internal network, a hacked public server would give a way straight in.
9: 1. A DMZ is an area where servers exposed to the external network (web, mail) are placed separately from the internal network. If one of those servers is attacked, the damage does not reach the internal network.

2. Traditional security trusts users inside the perimeter and checks only at the boundary. Zero trust trusts no one automatically — even inside the network, identity and permissions are verified every time.
10: 1 · Network entry — block unauthorized communication with a firewall
2 · Communication path — encrypt communication with a VPN
3 · Server placement — separate public-facing servers with a DMZ
4 · Endpoints — install antivirus software and keep the OS updated
11: (3) B — the firewall at the network entry

12.model: A firewall monitors the traffic at the entry/exit point of a network (it can also sit between parts of a network or on a host) and allows or denies each communication according to rules set in advance. For example, it can allow outside users to reach the public web server but deny any direct access from outside to the database server, so the database is never exposed to the Internet.
points: Sits at the network's entry/exit point (or between parts / on a host) (1)
Allows or denies communication (1)
According to rules set in advance (1)
Database example: allow the web server, deny direct external access to the database (1)

13.model: A VPN is an encrypted virtual private line, or tunnel, created over a public network such as the Internet, so that a remote user can connect safely to an organization's network. On public Wi-Fi other people can try to read the traffic, but with a VPN the content is encrypted inside the tunnel, so an eavesdropper sees only scrambled data. The risk of eavesdropping is therefore reduced.
points: Encrypted virtual private line / tunnel over the Internet (1)
Lets a remote user connect safely (1)
The content is encrypted (1)
So an eavesdropper on public Wi-Fi cannot read it (1)

14.model: Zero trust does not trust any user or device automatically just because it is inside the network or belongs to the organization. Every time a resource is requested, it checks identity (who is asking), permissions (whether they are allowed this resource) and context (whether the request fits — the device, the place, the time), according to the organization's policy. Only then is access given, and the check is repeated for each access.
points: No automatic trust from being inside the network (1)
Identity is checked (1)
Permissions are checked (1)
Context is checked, every time access is requested (1)

15.model: Traditional security protected a perimeter, on the idea that inside the organization's network is safe and outside is dangerous. With cloud services, data and systems sit outside the office network; with remote work, staff connect from home and from public places. The line between inside and outside has therefore blurred, so a design that protects only the perimeter leaves gaps — which is why zero trust verifies every access instead.

Cloud services put data and systems outside the network (1)
Remote work puts users outside the network (1)
So the boundary blurs and perimeter-only protection is not enough (1)
A zero-trust measure, with where it helps (e.g. verify each doctor's identity and permissions every time they open records) (1)
A defense-in-depth measure, with where it helps (e.g. a VPN for doctors at home; updated devices) (1)
Each placed correctly (1)
One risk that could remain, with a reason (e.g. a doctor's own device is infected; a stolen password) (1)
Three assets with a threat each (website attacked; remote staff eavesdropped; database leaked) (1)
A top layer chosen for this company, with a reason (1)
A layered design recommended (1)
Two reasons why layering is safer than one firewall (1)

18.model: Each measure guards a different point. The firewall, at the network entry, allows or denies communication by rules. The VPN protects the communication path by encrypting remote connections. The DMZ governs server placement, keeping public-facing servers apart so an attack on them cannot reach the internal network. Endpoint controls — antivirus and an updated OS — protect each device. Because they are at different points, an attacker who gets past one still faces the next, which is what defense in depth means.

8.q: 1. What a VPN is, and two uses
8.a: A VPN creates an encrypted virtual private line (a tunnel) over the Internet for safe connection from a remote location. Uses: remote work (connecting from home or while away) and connecting branches (offices in different places).
8.ar: خط مشفر عبر الإنترنت — للشغل من البيت ولربط الفروع.

8.a: In a DMZ, the public server is separated from the internal network, so if it is attacked the attacker cannot go on to the internal network and its confidential data. Inside the internal network, a hacked public server would give a way straight in.
8.ar: لو الخادم العام اتخرق، المهاجم ميقدرش يكمل للشبكة الداخلية.

9.q: 1. What a DMZ is and how it protects
9.a: A DMZ is an area where servers exposed to the external network (web, mail) are placed separately from the internal network. If one of those servers is attacked, the damage does not reach the internal network.
9.ar: عزل الخوادم العامة بيحمي اللي جوه.

9.a: Traditional security trusts users inside the perimeter and checks only at the boundary. Zero trust trusts no one automatically — even inside the network, identity and permissions are verified every time.
9.ar: التقليدي بيثق في اللي جوه، وانعدام الثقة بيتحقق من الكل كل مرة.

11.a: B — blocking unauthorized communication with a firewall.

12.a: A firewall monitors the traffic at the entry/exit point of a network (it can also sit between parts of a network or on a host) and allows or denies each communication according to rules set in advance. For example, it can allow outside users to reach the public web server but deny any direct access from outside to the database server, so the database is never exposed to the Internet.
12.ar: جدار الحماية بيقرر: يسمح ولا يمنع، حسب قواعد — ويمنع أي حد من برّه يوصل لقاعدة البيانات مباشرة.

13.a: A VPN is an encrypted virtual private line, or tunnel, created over a public network such as the Internet, so that a remote user can connect safely to an organization's network. On public Wi-Fi other people can try to read the traffic, but with a VPN the content is encrypted inside the tunnel, so an eavesdropper sees only scrambled data. The risk of eavesdropping is therefore reduced.
13.ar: النفق المشفر بيخلي اللي بيتصنت يشوف بيانات متلخبطة بس.

14.a: Zero trust does not trust any user or device automatically just because it is inside the network or belongs to the organization. Every time a resource is requested, it checks identity (who is asking), permissions (whether they are allowed this resource) and context (whether the request fits — the device, the place, the time), according to the organization's policy. Only then is access given, and the check is repeated for each access.

15.a: Traditional security protected a perimeter, on the idea that inside the organization's network is safe and outside is dangerous. With cloud services, data and systems sit outside the office network; with remote work, staff connect from home and from public places. The line between inside and outside has therefore blurred, so a design that protects only the perimeter leaves gaps — which is why zero trust verifies every access instead.
15.ar: السحابة والشغل من البيت مسحوا الحد بين الداخل والخارج.

16.a: One possible answer. Measure 1 (zero trust): every time a doctor opens a record, their identity and permissions are verified — so being logged in once is not enough. Measure 2 (defense in depth): doctors connect from home through a VPN, so the records cannot be read on the way, and their devices have antivirus and updates. One risk that could remain: a doctor's password could be stolen, or their home computer infected — no design is absolute.
16.ar: مثال لإجابة: إجراء لكل مفهوم، ومكانه، وخطر لسه موجود.

17.a: One possible answer. Assets and threats: the public website could be attacked; remote staff could be eavesdropped on; the customer database could be leaked. Most important layer: server placement — putting the website in a DMZ, because it is the most exposed asset and an attack on it must not reach the database. Design: a firewall, a VPN for remote staff, a DMZ for the website, and antivirus and updates on every device, with zero trust checking each access. Two reasons: if one layer is breached the next still protects the system; and each layer covers a different threat that a firewall alone does not.
17.ar: مثال لإجابة: الأصول والتهديدات، والطبقة الأهم بسبب، وتصميم بسببين.

18.a: Each measure guards a different point. The firewall, at the network entry, allows or denies communication by rules. The VPN protects the communication path by encrypting remote connections. The DMZ governs server placement, keeping public-facing servers apart so an attack on them cannot reach the internal network. Endpoint controls — antivirus and an updated OS — protect each device. Because they are at different points, an attacker who gets past one still faces the next, which is what defense in depth means.
18.ar: كل إجراء بيحمي نقطة مختلفة — ولو واحد اتعدّى، اللي بعده لسه موجود.

19.a: One possible answer. Extra measure: a VPN for staff who work from home, so their communication is encrypted. A threat it would still not remove: a member of staff tricked into giving away their password — the VPN protects the connection, not the password.
19.ar: أي إجراء مناسب، مع تهديد فعلًا هيفضل موجود.

20.a: One possible answer. The endpoints, because they depend on every user: one person who skips an update or opens an infected file can let an attacker in, however strong the other layers are.
